# How to use this guide

Pharmacology II (BP503T) is the continuation of Pharmacology I. Where Pharmacology I focused on general pharmacological principles, autonomic drugs, CVS drugs, CNS drugs, and autacoids, Pharmacology II covers the drugs used in antimicrobial therapy (antibacterials, antifungals, antivirals, anthelmintics, antiprotozoals) and antineoplastic agents, alongside the ANS and autacoids that link both courses. It is a subject that requires systematic memorisation — there are many drug classes and each requires you to know mechanism, classification, uses, pharmacokinetics, and adverse effects.

## Exam pattern

BP503T is examined at the end of Semester 5 as a **theory paper** following the PCI B.Pharm end-semester exam format.

**Typical PCI B.Pharm end-semester theory paper (75 marks, 3 hours)**

| Section | Type | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 10 short-answer questions — attempt all | 10 × 2 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 4 questions | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short notes — attempt 5 of 8 questions | 5 × 7 = 35 |
| **Total** | | **75** |

Confirm the exact format with your institution, as universities may vary the section types and counts. Some papers use multiple-choice questions in Section A.

## How the unit files are arranged

The PCI 2014 syllabus for BP503T has five units. This pack keeps **one notes file per unit**.

| Notes file | Unit | Key topics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 — ANS and Autacoids | I | Sympathomimetics, sympatholytics, parasympathomimetics, parasympatholytics, neuromuscular junction, ganglionic, histamine, 5-HT, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, bradykinin |
| Unit 2 — CNS Drugs | II | General anaesthetics, local anaesthetics, sedatives and hypnotics, antiepileptics, antipsychotics, antidepressants, anti-Parkinsonian, analgesics, NSAIDs |
| Unit 3 — CVS Drugs | III | Cardiac glycosides, antihypertensives, antianginals, antiarrhythmics, heart failure drugs, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, thrombolytics, hypolipidaemics |
| Unit 4 — Respiratory, GI, Renal | IV | Bronchodilators, antiasthmatics, antitussives, expectorants, GI drugs (H₂ blockers, PPIs, prokinetics, antidiarrhoeas, laxatives), diuretics, uricosurics |
| Unit 5 — Chemotherapy | V | Antibacterials (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines, macrolides, quinolones, sulphonamides), antifungals, antivirals, anthelmintics, antiprotozoals (antimalarials, antiamoebics), anticancer drugs |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Learn every drug class as a table.** For each class: mechanism of action → classification with examples → uses → pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) → adverse effects → contraindications → interactions. Use the same format every time.

2. **Mechanism of action is 2–3 marks.** Even in a 7-mark short note, a clear one-sentence mechanism with a diagram (where applicable) earns 2–3 marks before you have written anything else.

3. **Link mechanism to toxicity.** Most serious drug toxicities are extensions of the mechanism: aminoglycoside ototoxicity is because cochlear hair cells concentrate the drug; cisplatin nephrotoxicity is because the drug crosses the GFR freely and concentrates in the tubules. Knowing why helps you remember and write convincingly.

4. **For chemotherapy**: focus on (a) classification by mechanism (CCS vs CCNS); (b) one example per class with its unique toxicity (cyclophosphamide → haemorrhagic cystitis; bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis; vincristine → neuropathy; doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy); (c) the rationale for combination regimens.

5. **For antimicrobials**: master the β-lactam family first (penicillins and cephalosporins, their generations and spectra), then aminoglycosides (oto/nephrotoxic), fluoroquinolones (tendinitis, contraindicated in children), and tetracyclines (chelation, avoid in children/pregnancy). These are the most examined.

6. **For antiprotozoals**: always state which phase of the parasite life cycle the drug acts on; for malaria drugs, note chloroquine resistance and the role of ACTs.

7. **Adverse effects that examiners always test**: aminoglycoside ototoxicity, tetracycline tooth discolouration, fluoroquinolone tendon rupture, sulphonamide Stevens-Johnson syndrome, amphotericin nephrotoxicity, bleomycin pulmonary fibrosis, cisplatin nephrotoxicity, doxorubicin cardiomyopathy, vincristine neuropathy.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — asked in most years; commit the full answer to memory.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a broader question.
- **Low** — appears rarely; useful for MCQs and to round off a long essay.

These ratings are estimates based on PCI syllabus weightings and common exam patterns. They are a guide, not a guarantee.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | High-probability topics |
| --- | --- |
| 1 ANS + Autacoids | Adrenergic agonists and antagonists (classification + use), antihistamines, NSAIDs mechanism |
| 2 CNS | General anaesthetics (stages), benzodiazepines, antipsychotics (classification), opioid analgesics (mechanism + tolerance + naloxone) |
| 3 CVS | Cardiac glycosides (mechanism + toxicity), antihypertensives (5 groups + first-line choices), statins, anticoagulants (heparin vs warfarin) |
| 4 Respiratory/GI/Renal | Bronchodilators (β₂ agonists + mechanism), PPIs, loop diuretics (mechanism) |
| 5 Chemotherapy | β-Lactam antibiotics (penicillins + generations), aminoglycosides (ototoxicity), antimalarials (chloroquine + ACTs), anticancer classification + unique toxicities |

# Last-night revision sheet

Focus your final hour on five answers: **β-lactam antibiotics (penicillin mechanism + generations of cephalosporins)**, **aminoglycoside pharmacology (mechanism + ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity)**, **antimalarial drugs (chloroquine + ACTs with life-cycle stages)**, **classification of anticancer drugs with one example per class and its unique toxicity**, and **fluoroquinolone mechanism + adverse effects**. These cover the most-tested long and short questions.

---

## Mechanisms — one line each

| Drug / Class | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems | Inhibit PBPs (transpeptidase) → block peptidoglycan cross-linking → cell wall lysis (bactericidal) |
| Vancomycin | Binds D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursor → blocks transglycosylation (bactericidal; Gram-positive only) |
| Aminoglycosides | Bind 30S ribosome → misreading of mRNA → faulty proteins → bactericidal; require O₂ for entry |
| Tetracyclines | Bind 30S ribosome → block aminoacyl-tRNA binding → bacteriostatic |
| Macrolides | Bind 50S ribosome → block translocation → bacteriostatic |
| Clindamycin | Bind 50S ribosome → bacteriostatic; anaerobes + Gram-positive; risk: *C. difficile* colitis |
| Fluoroquinolones | Inhibit DNA gyrase (Gram-negative) and topo IV (Gram-positive) → DNA strand breaks → bactericidal |
| Sulphonamides | Block DHPS → prevent PABA → no dihydrofolate synthesis |
| Trimethoprim | Block DHFR → no THF → no purine/pyrimidine synthesis (synergistic with sulphonamide) |
| Amphotericin B | Binds ergosterol → membrane pores → cell content leak → fungicidal |
| Azole antifungals | Inhibit CYP51 (14α-lanosterol demethylase) → ergosterol depletion → fungistatic |
| Aciclovir | Phosphorylated by viral TK → inhibits viral DNA polymerase (chain terminator) |
| Chloroquine | Prevents haem polymerisation in parasite food vacuole → toxic haem accumulates |
| Artesunate | Generates free radicals → damages parasite proteins |
| Metronidazole | Activated by anaerobic organisms → reactive radical → DNA strand breaks |
| Mebendazole/albendazole | Bind β-tubulin → impair microtubule polymerisation → impair glucose uptake in helminths |
| Alkylating agents | Alkylate guanine → DNA cross-links → replication blocked (CCNS) |
| Antimetabolites | Interfere with DNA/RNA synthesis (CCS, S-phase); MTX: folate antagonist; 5-FU: thymidylate synthase |
| Vinca alkaloids | Bind tubulin → prevent polymerisation → mitotic arrest (CCS, M-phase) |
| Taxanes | Stabilise polymerised microtubules → prevent depolymerisation → mitotic arrest (CCS, M-phase) |
| Anthracyclines | Intercalate DNA + inhibit Topo II + free radicals (CCNS) |
| Platinum compounds | Intrastrand/interstrand DNA cross-links (CCNS) |

---

## Penicillin generations — at a glance

| Group | Example | Spectrum |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural | Benzylpenicillin (Pen G, IV) | Streptococcus, syphilis, gas gangrene |
| Antistaphylococcal | Cloxacillin | MSSA (β-lactamase-producing Staph) |
| Aminopenicillin | Amoxicillin | Gram-positive + H. influenzae, E. coli |
| + BLI | Co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin + clavulanate) | Resistant organisms; ENT, RTI, UTI |
| Antipseudomonal | Piperacillin-tazobactam | Gram-negative including Pseudomonas |

## Cephalosporin generations — at a glance

| Generation | Example | Cover note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1st | Cephalexin (oral), cefazolin (IV) | Gram-positive; MSSA; UTI, skin |
| 2nd | Cefuroxime | + H. influenzae, Moraxella; sinusitis |
| 3rd | Ceftriaxone (IV), cefixime (oral) | Extended Gram-negative; meningitis, typhoid |
| 4th | Cefepime | + Pseudomonas; hospital infections |
| 5th | Ceftaroline | MRSA; complicated skin |

---

## Adverse effects that always appear in exams

| Drug | Important ADR | Mnemonic / note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aminoglycosides | Ototoxicity (irreversible), nephrotoxicity | Monitor levels; avoid furosemide |
| Tetracyclines | Tooth discolouration, photosensitivity | Avoid < 8 yr, pregnancy |
| Fluoroquinolones | Tendinitis / tendon rupture (Achilles), cartilage damage | Avoid in children, athletes on steroids |
| Clindamycin | *C. difficile* pseudomembranous colitis | Treat with metronidazole or vancomycin |
| Sulphonamides | Stevens-Johnson syndrome, haemolysis in G6PD deficiency | Chelation with dairy/antacids irrelevant here |
| Amphotericin B | Nephrotoxicity, infusion reactions (fever, rigors), hypokalaemia | Liposomal form safer; premedicate |
| Metronidazole | Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste | Avoid alcohol |
| Chloroquine | Retinopathy (long-term), haemolysis in G6PD | Test for G6PD before primaquine |
| Primaquine | Haemolysis in G6PD deficiency | Test G6PD; CI in pregnancy |
| Cyclophosphamide | Haemorrhagic cystitis | Prevent with mesna + hydration |
| Cisplatin | Nephrotoxicity (severe), ototoxicity, nausea/vomiting | Hydrate before and after; use anti-emetics |
| Doxorubicin | Cardiomyopathy (cumulative, lifetime dose limit) | Monitor LVEF; vesicant |
| Bleomycin | Pulmonary fibrosis | Monitor DLCO; not myelosuppressive |
| Vincristine | Peripheral neuropathy (dose-limiting) | Not myelosuppressive; constipation |
| Methotrexate | Mucositis, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity | Folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue |
| L-Asparaginase | Hypersensitivity, pancreatitis, coagulopathy | Test dose first |

---

## Antimalarial drugs — by life-cycle phase

```text
Life cycle:
  Sporozoite (bite) → Liver (exoerythrocytic) → Merozoite
  → Red blood cell (erythrocytic: ring → trophozoite → schizont → merozoite + gametocyte)

Drugs by phase:
  Liver (tissue schizontocidal): primaquine, artemisinin (partial)
  Blood (erythrocytic / blood schizontocidal): chloroquine, quinine, artesunate, mefloquine
  Liver dormant stages (hypnozoites in P. vivax / P. ovale): primaquine only → "radical cure"
  Gametocytocidal: primaquine
```

**First-line treatment:**
- Falciparum: ACT (artemether-lumefantrine or artesunate-amodiaquine); artesunate IV for severe malaria
- Vivax/Ovale: chloroquine (radical cure with primaquine)

---

## Anticancer — class + unique toxicity (exam minimum)

| Class | Example | Unique toxicity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alkylating | Cyclophosphamide | Haemorrhagic cystitis (mesna); infertility |
| Platinum | Cisplatin | Nephrotoxicity + ototoxicity |
| Antimetabolite | Methotrexate | Mucositis; folinic acid rescue |
| Antimetabolite | 5-Fluorouracil | Mucositis; hand-foot syndrome |
| Vinca alkaloid | Vincristine | Peripheral neuropathy; not myelosuppressive |
| Taxane | Paclitaxel | Neuropathy + neutropenia; hypersensitivity (premedicate) |
| Anthracycline | Doxorubicin | Cardiomyopathy (dose-limited); vesicant |
| Topoisomerase I | Irinotecan | Delayed diarrhoea (atropine for early; loperamide for late) |
| Bleomycin | Bleomycin | Pulmonary fibrosis; NOT myelosuppressive |
| Hormonal | Tamoxifen | Endometrial cancer, DVT |

**CCS vs CCNS**:
- CCS (cell-cycle specific, kills only dividing cells): antimetabolites (S), vinca alkaloids (M), taxanes (M), bleomycin (G2/M)
- CCNS (kills resting and dividing): alkylating agents, platinum, anthracyclines

---

## Exam reminder

- Section A (20 marks, 10 × 2): expect one 2-mark answer per drug class — mechanism of one drug, one ADR, one use. Write precisely.
- Section B (20 marks, 2 × 10): classification questions are common — name 3–4 classes, one drug each, mechanism, uses. Tables earn marks efficiently.
- Section C (35 marks, 5 × 7): short notes typically ask you to write about one drug class (write mechanism → classification with examples → uses → ADR → contraindications in that order, 7 marks = 7 clear points).
- For every antibiotic short note: state bactericidal vs bacteriostatic and why (linking mechanism to activity tells the examiner you understand the pharmacology, not just memorised the fact).
- Never confuse mechanism with use: "blocks 30S ribosome" is mechanism; "used for atypical pneumonia" is clinical use; write both.

mcqs.explanation: β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle mediate relaxation and bronchodilation when stimulated by adrenaline or selective β2 agonists such as salbutamol.
mcqs.question: Which receptor subtype is primarily responsible for the bronchodilator effect of adrenaline?

mcqs.explanation: Adrenaline acts on α1 (raises BP, reduces urticaria), β1 (improves cardiac output) and β2 (reverses bronchoconstriction and inhibits mast cell mediator release) receptors, addressing all major manifestations of anaphylaxis.
options: Reverses bronchoconstriction, hypotension and urticaria via adrenergic receptors
mcqs.question: Adrenaline is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis because it:

mcqs.explanation: Propranolol is a non-selective β blocker. Blockade of β2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle removes the bronchodilatory tone and can precipitate life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatic patients.
mcqs.question: Propranolol is contraindicated in bronchial asthma because it blocks:

mcqs.explanation: Prazosin selectively blocks post-synaptic α1 receptors. Because presynaptic α2 autoreceptors are spared, the baroreceptor reflex is partly intact, but on the first dose the sudden vasodilation before baroreceptors compensate can cause syncope.
options: Selective α1 blockade causing venodilation and loss of compensatory vasoconstriction
mcqs.question: The first-dose postural hypotension seen with prazosin is due to:

mcqs.explanation: 'Mad as a hatter' refers to central muscarinic blockade causing confusion, agitation and delirium. The other signs are peripheral: dry mouth (dry as a bone), tachycardia, flushing (red as a beet), hyperthermia (hot as a hare) and mydriasis (blind as a bat).
mcqs.question: Atropine toxicity is remembered by the mnemonic 'Mad as a hatter'. Which sign represents the CNS component?

mcqs.explanation: Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and raises acetylcholine at all cholinergic synapses. Excess ACh at muscarinic receptors causes bradycardia, bronchospasm and hypersalivation. Atropine pre-treatment blocks these muscarinic effects without blocking the nicotinic NMJ effect that reverses the block.
options: Atropine potentiates neostigmine at the NMJ
Atropine blocks excessive muscarinic side effects of neostigmine
mcqs.question: Neostigmine must always be given with atropine when reversing neuromuscular blockade because:

mcqs.explanation: Pilocarpine (a muscarinic M3 agonist) causes miosis (pupil constriction) and contraction of the ciliary muscle, which pulls the trabecular meshwork open and increases conventional aqueous drainage, reducing intraocular pressure.
options: Cause miosis and open the trabecular meshwork increasing aqueous outflow
Dilate the pupil reducing intraocular pressure
Reduce aqueous humour production via β2 blockade
Increase uveoscleral outflow via prostaglandin release
mcqs.question: Pilocarpine eye drops are used in glaucoma because they:

mcqs.explanation: Dobutamine is a selective β1 agonist used as an IV inotrope in acute heart failure. It increases cardiac contractility and output with minimal effect on heart rate and peripheral resistance compared to adrenaline.
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a selective β1 adrenergic agonist used in cardiac failure?

mcqs.explanation: COX-1 is constitutively expressed and produces prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) that protect the gastric mucosa by stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion. COX-1 inhibition reduces these protective prostaglandins, predisposing to ulceration.
mcqs.question: COX-1 inhibition by NSAIDs is responsible for:

mcqs.explanation: Second-generation H1 antihistamines are more polar (zwitterionic) and cross the blood-brain barrier poorly, so they cause minimal CNS sedation and psychomotor impairment compared to first-generation agents.
options: Are more potent at H1 receptors
Have a longer duration of action via depot effect
Block both H1 and H2 receptors
Do not cross the blood-brain barrier and cause less sedation
mcqs.question: Second-generation antihistamines (e.g. cetirizine) are preferred over first-generation because they:

mcqs.explanation: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions) while pralidoxime regenerates the enzyme if given early (before 'ageing' of the bond). Both are used together.
mcqs.question: The antidote for organophosphate poisoning is:

mcqs.explanation: Bradykinin directly activates pain receptors (B2 receptors) and stimulates prostaglandin synthesis. PGE2 sensitises nociceptors (peripheral sensitisation) and acts on the hypothalamus to raise the thermoregulatory set-point (fever).
mcqs.question: Which autacoid is primarily responsible for pain and pyrexia of inflammation?

mcqs.explanation: Aspirin covalently acetylates the COX active site. Platelets are anucleate; they cannot make new protein. So once aspirin inhibits their COX, the effect is permanent for each platelet's lifespan of 7–10 days.
options: Aspirin has a long half-life of 7 days
Platelets are anucleate and cannot synthesise new COX protein
Platelets have high baseline COX activity
mcqs.question: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX. The platelet effect lasts 7–10 days because:

mcqs.explanation: While celecoxib itself is not the main concern here, combining celecoxib with warfarin requires careful INR monitoring as NSAIDs can displace warfarin from plasma proteins and inhibit its metabolism (CYP2C9 inhibition by some NSAIDs), increasing bleeding risk.
mcqs.question: Which drug should NEVER be combined with a selective COX-2 inhibitor (e.g. celecoxib) in a patient on low-dose aspirin?

mcqs.explanation: At high doses dopamine activates α1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasoconstriction, raised peripheral resistance and increased BP. The renal dopaminergic vasodilation seen at low doses is overwhelmed.
options: D1 dopamine receptors causing renal vasodilation
mcqs.question: Dopamine at high doses (>10 μg/kg/min) primarily activates:

mcqs.explanation: Clonidine stimulates presynaptic α2 receptors in the vasomotor centre of the brainstem, reducing sympathetic outflow and lowering blood pressure. It is used for hypertension and opioid withdrawal.
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a selective α2 agonist used as a centrally acting antihypertensive?

mcqs.explanation: Carcinoid tumours release large amounts of serotonin, causing the triad of flushing, diarrhoea and bronchospasm. Treatment involves octreotide (somatostatin analogue) to reduce 5-HT secretion.
options: Hypertension via 5-HT3 receptors in the vasomotor centre
Carcinoid syndrome — flushing, diarrhoea and bronchospasm from excess 5-HT
mcqs.question: Serotonin (5-HT) is involved in which of the following conditions? (Select most accurate answer)

mcqs.explanation: Non-selective beta blockers (propranolol) block β2 vasodilation. When adrenaline is given, only α1 vasoconstriction occurs (unopposed) → severe hypertension and reflex bradycardia.
options: Unopposed α1 stimulation from adrenaline causes a hypertensive crisis
mcqs.question: Adrenaline must be used with CAUTION in patients taking non-selective beta blockers because:

mcqs.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist. It blocks bradycardia, bronchospasm, hypersalivation and GI hypermotility caused by excess acetylcholine from neostigmine's cholinesterase inhibition.
mcqs.question: Which drug is the antidote for excess muscarinic effects of neostigmine?

mcqs.explanation: COX-2 inhibitors reduce PGI2 (a vasodilator and platelet-aggregation inhibitor) while sparing TXA2 production (a vasoconstrictor and aggregator), creating a prothrombotic state. Rofecoxib increased MI risk and was withdrawn in 2004.
mcqs.question: The major adverse effect of selective COX-2 inhibitors (coxibs) that led to withdrawal of rofecoxib is:

mcqs.explanation: MAC is the alveolar concentration (in % at 1 atm) that prevents movement in 50% of subjects in response to a standard surgical incision. It is inversely related to potency — a lower MAC means the drug is more potent (less drug is needed).
options: Potency (the lower the MAC, the more potent)
mcqs.question: The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of an inhaled anaesthetic is a measure of its:

mcqs.explanation: Thiopentone is a potent inducer of hepatic ALA (aminolaevulinic acid) synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme in haem synthesis. In porphyria, this leads to accumulation of toxic porphyrin precursors (ALA, PBG), causing acute neurological crises.
options: Induces delta-ALA synthase → accumulation of porphyrin precursors
mcqs.question: Thiopentone sodium is contraindicated in acute intermittent porphyria because it:

mcqs.explanation: Ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors, causing a dissociative state with analgesia, amnesia and muscle tone preserved. It is unique as an anaesthetic that maintains cardiovascular and respiratory function and is bronchodilatory.
mcqs.question: Ketamine produces 'dissociative anaesthesia' by acting as an antagonist at:

mcqs.explanation: Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators: they bind at the α-γ interface of GABA-A and increase the frequency of Cl- channel opening in response to GABA. Barbiturates increase duration. Neither acts without GABA (at clinical doses).
options: Increasing the duration of Cl- channel opening
Blocking the Cl- channel at high concentrations
Directly opening the Cl- channel in the absence of GABA
Increasing the frequency of Cl- channel opening
mcqs.question: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor function by:

mcqs.explanation: In physically dependent patients, flumazenil abruptly removes benzodiazepine receptor occupancy and precipitates acute withdrawal, which can cause refractory seizures. It is also contraindicated if benzodiazepines are being used to control epilepsy.
options: Patients who are physically dependent on benzodiazepines (precipitates seizures)
mcqs.question: Flumazenil is the specific antidote for benzodiazepine overdose. It should NOT be used in:

mcqs.explanation: Zero-order (saturation) kinetics means the metabolising enzyme (CYP2C9) is saturated at therapeutic levels. The same absolute amount is metabolised per unit time regardless of concentration. A small dose increase in the therapeutic range dramatically raises plasma levels.
options: A fixed fraction of the drug is eliminated per unit time
A fixed amount of drug is eliminated per unit time — a small dose increase can cause a large jump in plasma levels
Elimination is independent of plasma concentration at all levels
mcqs.question: Phenytoin exhibits zero-order kinetics at therapeutic plasma levels. This means that:

mcqs.explanation: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia in 20% of patients, particularly in those with poor oral hygiene. It is thought to be due to the drug stimulating fibroblast proliferation in gum tissue. Regular dental hygiene and check-ups are essential.
mcqs.question: Gingival hyperplasia is a characteristic chronic adverse effect of:

mcqs.explanation: Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures. They must be avoided in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and typical absence epilepsy. Valproate and ethosuximide are the drugs of choice for absence seizures.
mcqs.question: Which antiepileptic is contraindicated in absence seizures because it can worsen them?

mcqs.explanation: The nigrostriatal pathway regulates movement. Blocking D2 receptors here disrupts the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the striatum → EPS (dystonia, parkinsonism, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia).
mcqs.question: Extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) of antipsychotics are caused by dopamine D2 receptor blockade in which pathway?

mcqs.explanation: Clozapine causes agranulocytosis in 1–2% of patients, which can be fatal if undetected. All patients require weekly WBC monitoring for 18 weeks, then fortnightly. Despite this, its superior efficacy in resistant schizophrenia justifies use.
mcqs.question: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia because it requires regular blood monitoring for:

mcqs.explanation: NMS is a rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics. The hallmarks are hyperthermia (often >40°C), lead-pipe muscle rigidity, altered consciousness, and autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile blood pressure). CK is markedly elevated.
options: Hyperthermia, generalised muscle rigidity, altered consciousness with autonomic instability
mcqs.question: The neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) triad is:

mcqs.explanation: SSRIs selectively inhibit the serotonin transporter (SERT) on presynaptic neurons, preventing reuptake of serotonin from the synapse and increasing synaptic 5-HT concentration.
options: Selectively block the serotonin (SERT) reuptake transporter
Block reuptake of noradrenaline at the nerve terminal
mcqs.question: The mechanism of SSRIs is:

mcqs.explanation: Tolerance develops readily to analgesia, sedation, respiratory depression, nausea and euphoria. Constipation (reduced GI motility) and miosis (pupillary constriction) are opioid effects that persist with chronic use — a laxative should always be co-prescribed.
mcqs.question: Which opioid effect does NOT develop tolerance with chronic use?

mcqs.explanation: Morphine-induced respiratory depression causes CO2 retention (hypercapnia), which is a potent cerebral vasodilator. Raised PaCO2 increases cerebral blood flow and further elevates an already raised intracranial pressure, worsening brain herniation risk.
options: It blocks opioid receptors in the medulla
Respiratory depression raises PaCO2 → cerebral vasodilation → raised intracranial pressure
mcqs.question: Morphine should be used with great caution in head injuries because:

mcqs.explanation: Local anaesthetics are weak bases (pKa ~8). Unionised form crosses the axonal membrane. Infected tissue is acidic → more drug in ionised form → less membrane penetration → reduced efficacy. Larger doses are needed but should not be exceeded.
options: Blood flow is reduced, lowering drug delivery
Acidic pH of inflamed tissue keeps the drug ionised, reducing membrane penetration
Inflammatory mediators compete at the Na+ channel
mcqs.question: Local anaesthetics are LESS effective in infected tissue because:

mcqs.explanation: Adrenaline (1:200,000) causes α1 vasoconstriction at the injection site, reducing vascular absorption of the local anaesthetic. This prolongs its duration, allows a higher total dose, and reduces bleeding. Adrenaline-containing solutions must NOT be used for ring blocks (fingers, toes, penis) due to ischaemia risk.
options: Cause local vasoconstriction, reduce bleeding and prolong duration of action
mcqs.question: Adrenaline is added to local anaesthetic solutions to:

mcqs.explanation: MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) prevent serotonin breakdown by MAO. Combining with SSRIs causes massive 5-HT accumulation → serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, clonus, diaphoresis, agitation, autonomic instability — can be fatal). A 2-week washout of MAOI is required before starting an SSRI; with fluoxetine (long half-life of 5 weeks) a 5-week SSRI washout is needed before starting an MAOI.
mcqs.question: Which antidepressant class requires a 2-week washout before starting an SSRI due to risk of serotonin syndrome?

mcqs.explanation: Propofol infusion syndrome occurs at high infusion rates over extended periods, particularly in critically ill patients. Features include severe metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, hyperkalaemia and cardiac failure. The mechanism involves impaired mitochondrial function and fatty acid oxidation.
options: High doses (>5 mg/kg/h) for more than 48 hours
mcqs.question: Propofol infusion syndrome is a rare but fatal complication seen when propofol is given at:

mcqs.explanation: Carbamazepine is a potent inducer of its own metabolising enzymes (CYP3A4), a process called autoinduction. Over the first 3–4 weeks, its half-life shortens significantly, so the initial dose that achieves a therapeutic level may become subtherapeutic and require dose escalation.
mcqs.question: Carbamazepine inhibits its own metabolism over the first weeks of treatment. This is known as:

mcqs.explanation: Naloxone has a half-life of 30–60 minutes, shorter than most opioids (morphine ~6 hours). After initial reversal of respiratory depression, the patient can re-narcotise as naloxone wears off. Repeated IV boluses or a continuous infusion are often needed.
options: It has a shorter duration of action than most opioids
It is rapidly metabolised in the gut
mcqs.question: Naloxone, the opioid antidote, must often be repeated or given as an infusion because:

mcqs.explanation: K+ and digoxin bind at overlapping sites on the extracellular face of Na+/K+-ATPase. When serum K+ is low, there is less competition, digoxin binds more avidly to the pump, and inhibition is exaggerated, causing toxicity even at normal digoxin plasma levels.
options: K+ and digoxin compete for the same binding site on Na+/K+-ATPase — low K+ sensitises the pump to digoxin
mcqs.question: Digoxin toxicity is precipitated by hypokalaemia because:

mcqs.explanation: GI symptoms — anorexia (the earliest and most reliable marker), followed by nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea — appear before cardiac arrhythmias in digoxin toxicity. Yellow-green visual haloes (xanthopsia) are a classic CNS sign. Cardiac toxicity (arrhythmias) is the most dangerous manifestation.
mcqs.question: The earliest sign of digoxin toxicity is:

mcqs.explanation: ACE is identical to kininase II, the enzyme that inactivates bradykinin. ACE inhibition prevents bradykinin degradation. Accumulated bradykinin stimulates local prostaglandin synthesis and afferent sensory C-fibres in the lung, causing a persistent dry cough. Switching to an ARB avoids this side effect.
options: Accumulation of bradykinin in the lungs (not broken down because ACE is also kininase II)
mcqs.question: ACE inhibitors cause dry cough in 10–20% of patients due to:

mcqs.explanation: In bilateral renal artery stenosis, GFR is maintained by efferent arteriolar constriction by angiotensin II. ACE inhibitors remove this compensatory mechanism → efferent vasodilation → reduced glomerular filtration pressure → acute kidney injury.
options: They cause hyperkalaemia which worsens renal function
They block the angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction that maintains GFR, causing acute renal failure
They reduce renal blood flow via vasodilation
mcqs.question: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis because:

mcqs.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X. These factors affect the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, measured by prothrombin time. The INR standardises PT across laboratories. Target INR 2–3 for most indications.
options: International normalised ratio (INR) derived from prothrombin time
mcqs.question: Warfarin anticoagulant effect is monitored by:

mcqs.explanation: In HIT, the immune system generates IgG antibodies against the heparin-platelet factor 4 (PF4) complex. These antibodies bind FcγRIIA receptors on platelets, activating them → platelet aggregation and thrombus formation → thrombocytopenia from platelet consumption plus paradoxical thrombosis.
options: Heparin directly activates platelets via H1 receptors
Platelets are sequestered in the spleen
IgG antibodies to the heparin-PF4 complex activate platelets via FcγRIIA, causing widespread thrombosis
mcqs.question: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) is paradoxically a thrombotic rather than a bleeding complication because:

mcqs.explanation: Nitrate tolerance develops within 24 hours of continuous exposure due to depletion of tissue thiols (required for bioactivation) and neurohormonal counterregulation. A nitrate-free interval — typically removing the transdermal patch at night — allows enzyme and thiol recovery.
options: Providing an 8–12 hour nitrate-free interval daily
mcqs.question: Organic nitrates cause tolerance with continuous use. This is prevented by:

mcqs.explanation: Nitrates increase cGMP (via NO-guanylate cyclase) and sildenafil inhibits PDE5 (the enzyme that breaks down cGMP). The combination causes massive cGMP accumulation in vascular smooth muscle → profound vasodilation and potentially fatal hypotension.
options: Both cause tachycardia which is additive
Both elevate cGMP in vascular smooth muscle → severe synergistic hypotension
mcqs.question: Sildenafil is absolutely contraindicated with organic nitrates because:

mcqs.explanation: Amiodarone causes multi-organ toxicity due to its long half-life and iodine content. Thyroid dysfunction (hypo or hyperthyroidism from iodine load) and pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis → fibrosis) are the most important. Corneal microdeposits (almost universal) and hepatotoxicity also occur.
mcqs.question: The most important adverse effect of amiodarone requiring regular monitoring is:

mcqs.explanation: HMG-CoA reductase inhibition reduces hepatic cholesterol synthesis. The liver compensates by upregulating LDL receptors on hepatocytes, which avidly clear LDL particles from plasma. The net result is a 30–50% reduction in LDL-C.
options: Blocking LDL oxidation in the vessel wall
Inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase → reduced hepatic cholesterol → upregulated LDL receptors → increased LDL clearance
mcqs.question: Statins reduce LDL-cholesterol primarily by:

mcqs.explanation: Gemfibrozil inhibits glucuronidation and reduces renal excretion of active statin metabolites, dramatically raising their plasma levels. CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azole antifungals) similarly raise simvastatin and atorvastatin levels, increasing myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk.
options: Fibrates (especially gemfibrozil) or drugs inhibiting CYP3A4 such as erythromycin
mcqs.question: Statin-induced rhabdomyolysis is most likely when statins are combined with:

mcqs.explanation: Class III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide) block voltage-gated K+ channels → delayed repolarisation → prolonged action potential duration and refractory period → reduced re-entry arrhythmias. This shows as a prolonged QT interval on the ECG.
mcqs.question: Which Vaughan Williams class of antiarrhythmic blocks potassium channels to prolong the action potential?

mcqs.explanation: The mortality benefit of spironolactone in heart failure (RALES trial, 30% reduction) is largely attributed to its anti-fibrotic effect — blocking aldosterone receptors in the myocardium and blood vessels reduces pathological cardiac remodelling and fibrosis, independent of its relatively weak diuretic action.
options: Blocking aldosterone-mediated myocardial and vascular fibrosis (beyond its diuretic effect)
mcqs.question: Spironolactone reduces mortality in heart failure by:

mcqs.explanation: Warfarin crosses the placenta and inhibits foetal coagulation factor synthesis. In the first trimester it causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses). Later, it causes foetal haemorrhage. Heparin is used instead — it does not cross the placenta.
options: It is not absorbed orally during pregnancy
It crosses the placenta and inhibits foetal coagulation factor synthesis causing embryopathy and foetal haemorrhage
It is rapidly metabolised by placental enzymes
mcqs.question: Warfarin should NOT be used in pregnancy because:

mcqs.explanation: Clopidogrel requires CYP2C19-mediated hepatic conversion to its active metabolite, which then irreversibly alkylates the ADP P2Y12 receptor on platelets. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers have reduced antiplatelet efficacy, increasing the risk of stent thrombosis.
mcqs.question: Clopidogrel is a prodrug requiring activation by:

mcqs.explanation: Methyldopa is converted to α-methylnoradrenaline, which acts on central α2 receptors to reduce sympathetic outflow. It has the longest safety record in pregnancy, with follow-up studies showing no adverse foetal or childhood developmental effects.
options: It crosses the placenta and directly reduces foetal BP
It is an α2 agonist that is extensively studied and proven safe for the foetus
It is the most potent antihypertensive available
mcqs.question: Methyldopa is the antihypertensive of choice in pregnancy because:

mcqs.explanation: Carvedilol blocks β1, β2 and α1 receptors plus has antioxidant properties. In heart failure, its β1 blockade reduces heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand while its α1 blockade reduces afterload. The COPERNICUS trial showed it reduces mortality in severe HF.
options: Non-selective β blocker with additional α1 blockade and antioxidant properties
mcqs.question: Carvedilol is used in chronic heart failure because it is a:

mcqs.explanation: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab fragments) bind free digoxin in the plasma, rapidly reversing toxicity. Atropine and lignocaine treat specific arrhythmias (bradycardia and ventricular ectopics respectively) but do not remove the drug. Protamine reverses heparin, not digoxin.
mcqs.question: The antidote for severe digoxin toxicity is:

mcqs.explanation: Dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine) act predominantly on vascular smooth muscle L-type Ca2+ channels with relatively little effect on the heart. Verapamil and diltiazem (non-dihydropyridines) have significant rate-limiting effects on the SA and AV nodes.
mcqs.question: Which of the following calcium channel blockers selectively dilates coronary arteries without affecting heart rate?

mcqs.explanation: Digoxin slows the ventricular rate in AF by increasing vagal tone and slowing AV node conduction. Its positive inotropy makes it suitable when LV function is impaired. Verapamil and beta blockers can also control rate but are used with caution in impaired LV function.
mcqs.question: The drug of choice for controlling ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation in a patient with impaired LV function is:

mcqs.explanation: Salbutamol inhaled has an onset of 2–5 minutes and a duration of 4–6 hours. It is used as a reliever (rescue inhaler) for acute asthma symptoms. LABAs (salmeterol, formoterol) last 12 hours and are used as twice-daily controllers.
mcqs.question: Salbutamol is classified as a SABA. 'Short-acting' refers to its duration of bronchodilation, which is approximately:

mcqs.explanation: Above 20 mg/L: headache, nausea, insomnia, tremor and tachycardia. Above 25 mg/L: seizures (can be refractory) and ventricular arrhythmias (the most dangerous toxic effects). The therapeutic range is 10–20 mg/L.
mcqs.question: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index. The toxic signs at plasma levels >25 mg/L include:

mcqs.explanation: Drug deposition in the oropharynx allows Candida overgrowth. A spacer reduces oropharyngeal deposition by >70%. Rinsing the mouth with water and spitting after every dose removes residual drug. These measures significantly reduce local side effects without compromising lung deposition.
options: Using a spacer device and rinsing the mouth after every inhaler use
Adding an antifungal to the ICS inhaler
mcqs.question: A patient on inhaled corticosteroids develops oral thrush. The recommended prevention measure is:

mcqs.explanation: Ipratropium is a quaternary ammonium muscarinic antagonist. It blocks M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle (reducing ACh-mediated bronchoconstriction) and submucosal glands (reducing mucus secretion). It is poorly absorbed and does not cross the BBB, minimising systemic anticholinergic effects.
options: β2 receptor agonism in bronchial smooth muscle
Blocking muscarinic M3 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle and glands → reduced bronchoconstriction and secretions
mcqs.question: Ipratropium bromide acts as a bronchodilator by:

mcqs.explanation: PPIs are prodrugs that accumulate in the acidic parietal cell canaliculus and form a covalent bond with the active H+/K+-ATPase proton pump. The pump is activated by eating. Taking the PPI before the first meal ensures maximum pump activity when the drug arrives, maximising inhibition.
options: Their half-life is shortest in the fasting state
They require gastric acid for absorption
They need to reach the parietal cell before it is actively secreting acid — only active pumps are inhibited
mcqs.question: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) must be taken 30–60 minutes before a meal because:

mcqs.explanation: Standard first-line triple therapy: a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg) + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily for 7–14 days. The PPI reduces acid, improving antibiotic stability and efficacy in the stomach.
mcqs.question: The triple therapy for H. pylori eradication typically consists of:

mcqs.explanation: Cytotoxic drugs damage the GI mucosa, releasing serotonin (5-HT) from enterochromaffin cells. This activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, which signal to the vomiting centre. Ondansetron blocks these 5-HT3 receptors, interrupting this pathway.
options: Mast cells in the gut wall
The vomiting centre in the medulla
Enterochromaffin cells in the GI mucosa, which activates vagal 5-HT3 receptors
mcqs.question: Ondansetron is particularly effective for chemotherapy-induced nausea because chemotherapy releases serotonin from:

mcqs.explanation: Metoclopramide blocks D2 receptors both centrally (CTZ — antiemetic) and in the striatum (nigrostriatal — EPS). Young women are particularly susceptible to acute dystonias (oculogyric crisis, torticollis). Treatment: benztropine or diphenhydramine IM.
options: D2 antagonist in the basal ganglia/nigrostriatal system
mcqs.question: Metoclopramide can cause acute dystonia, particularly in young women, due to its action as a:

mcqs.explanation: Unlike thiazides, frusemide reaches the thick ascending limb via active secretion by the organic anion transport system in the proximal tubule. This mechanism is maintained even when GFR is low. Thiazides fail when GFR is <30 mL/min because they are not filtered in sufficient quantities.
options: It is filtered at the glomerulus and concentrated in the tubule
It increases GFR by dilating afferent arterioles
It acts on renal interstitium independently of tubular function
It is secreted by proximal tubular organic anion transporters and reaches the loop of Henle directly
mcqs.question: Frusemide (furosemide) is effective even in severe renal impairment (low GFR) because:

mcqs.explanation: Allopurinol reduces urate synthesis and gradually reduces plasma and tissue urate. If started during an acute attack, the rapid fall in plasma urate causes crystal mobilisation from tissues into the joint, prolonging or worsening inflammation. It should be started 2–4 weeks after the acute attack resolves.
options: Rapid mobilisation of urate crystals can prolong or worsen the acute attack
It worsens renal excretion of urate
It inhibits xanthine oxidase which worsens hyperuricaemia
It causes lactic acidosis when urate levels are high
mcqs.question: Allopurinol must NOT be started during an acute gout attack because:

mcqs.explanation: Lactulose is a disaccharide not absorbed from the gut. Colonic bacteria ferment it to short-chain fatty acids, lowering colonic pH. Acidification converts NH3 (which crosses colonic epithelium) to NH4+ (which cannot), reducing systemic ammonia absorption and improving encephalopathy.
options: Is metabolised by colonic bacteria to acidic products (lactic acid, acetic acid) → traps NH3 as NH4+ → reduces ammonia absorption
Directly detoxifies ammonia in the liver
mcqs.question: Lactulose is used in hepatic encephalopathy because it:

mcqs.explanation: Codeine (opioid) and dextromethorphan (NMDA antagonist) act centrally to suppress the cough reflex in the medullary cough centre. Bromhexine and guaifenesin are expectorants that act peripherally. Ammonium chloride is a traditional expectorant.
mcqs.question: Which antitussive acts centrally by suppressing the cough centre in the medulla?

mcqs.explanation: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion (less Ang II → less aldosterone → K+ retention). Spironolactone directly blocks the aldosterone receptor → further K+ retention. Combining them risks life-threatening hyperkalaemia, especially in patients with renal impairment.
mcqs.question: Spironolactone is contraindicated with ACE inhibitors without close monitoring because both cause:

mcqs.explanation: Thiazides stimulate Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, reducing urinary Ca2+ excretion. This is used to prevent calcium-oxalate renal stone formation in patients with hypercalciuria. Loop diuretics have the opposite effect and promote calciuria.
options: Treating osteoporosis by increasing bone calcium
Preventing calcium-oxalate kidney stones (reduce urinary calcium excretion)
mcqs.question: Thiazide diuretics are unique among diuretics in that they cause hypocalciuria. This property is clinically useful for:

mcqs.explanation: Cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) released from mast cells and eosinophils bind CysLT1 receptors in the airway, causing bronchoconstriction, oedema and mucus secretion. Montelukast specifically blocks CysLT1 receptors, reducing these effects.
options: CysLT1 receptors for cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4)
mcqs.question: Montelukast exerts its antiasthmatic effect by blocking:

mcqs.explanation: Both frusemide (high ceiling loop diuretic) and aminoglycosides are independently ototoxic. The combination is synergistically ototoxic — permanent cochlear and vestibular damage. The two should be avoided together where possible.
mcqs.question: Ototoxicity from rapid intravenous injection of frusemide is potentiated by:

mcqs.explanation: Sucralfate is an aluminium salt of sucrose octasulphate. In the acidic stomach it polymerises into a viscous gel that selectively adheres to the ulcer crater (which has a lower pH than normal mucosa), creating a physical protective barrier against acid and pepsin for 4–6 hours.
options: Blocking H2 receptors on parietal cells
Forming a viscous gel that adheres to ulcer base, protecting it from acid and pepsin
mcqs.question: Sucralfate works by:

mcqs.explanation: Undiagnosed abdominal pain with distension can indicate bowel obstruction or acute abdomen. Administering a laxative could worsen obstruction or cause bowel perforation. These patients require urgent surgical assessment before any laxative is given.
options: Undiagnosed abdominal pain and distension with nausea (possible bowel obstruction)
mcqs.question: A nurse should withhold a laxative and report to the prescriber if the patient presents with:

mcqs.explanation: Sodium cromoglicate prevents mast cell degranulation by blocking Cl- channels (reducing Ca2+ entry needed for exocytosis). When used before exercise or allergen exposure, it prevents the early and late asthmatic reactions. It has no bronchodilator activity — it must be used before the trigger, not during an attack.
options: Relaxing bronchial smooth muscle via β2 stimulation
Blocking muscarinic receptors in the bronchi
Inhibiting mast cell degranulation, preventing mediator release
mcqs.question: Sodium cromoglicate is used for prophylaxis of exercise-induced asthma. It acts by:

mcqs.explanation: The FDA-mandated LABA warning: clinical trials (SMART trial with salmeterol) showed increased risk of asthma-related deaths when LABAs were used as monotherapy. LABAs must always be combined with an ICS. The leading hypothesis is that LABAs mask worsening inflammation without treating it.
options: They cause bronchospasm with regular use
They have a short duration of action
Phase III trials showed increased asthma deaths when LABAs were used without inhaled corticosteroids
mcqs.question: Long-acting beta-2 agonists (LABAs) must NEVER be used as monotherapy in asthma because:

mcqs.explanation: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) bind to penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), which are transpeptidase enzymes that catalyse the final cross-linking step of peptidoglycan. Without cross-linking the cell wall is structurally weak, osmotic lysis occurs and the bacterium dies (bactericidal).
options: Inhibiting 30S ribosomal subunit → misreading of mRNA
Binding penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking
Increasing cell membrane permeability via ergosterol binding
mcqs.question: Beta-lactam antibiotics kill bacteria by:

mcqs.explanation: Most community Staphylococcus aureus strains produce a beta-lactamase (penicillinase) that cleaves the beta-lactam ring, inactivating the drug. This is overcome by: (a) penicillinase-resistant penicillins (cloxacillin), or (b) combining amoxicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (clavulanate).
options: Production of beta-lactamase (penicillinase) that hydrolyses the beta-lactam ring
mcqs.question: The most common mechanism of penicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus is:

mcqs.explanation: Aminoglycosides are concentrated in proximal tubular cells (nephrotoxicity) and cochlear hair cells (ototoxicity — both cochlear and vestibular). Toxicity is related to trough levels (sustained high exposure). Once-daily dosing maintains bactericidal peak concentration-dependent activity while reducing trough-related toxicity.
mcqs.question: The major toxicity of aminoglycosides that requires monitoring of trough levels is:

mcqs.explanation: Tetracyclines chelate calcium and are incorporated into developing teeth and bones. This causes permanent yellow-brown discolouration of deciduous and permanent teeth, dental enamel hypoplasia, and may retard bone growth in young children. They are also contraindicated in pregnancy (affects foetal dentition and bones).
options: Deposit in developing teeth and bone causing dental staining and enamel hypoplasia
mcqs.question: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8 years because they:

mcqs.explanation: Ethambutol causes retrochiasmal optic neuritis manifesting as reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green colour discrimination. It is dose-related and usually reversible if detected early. Baseline visual acuity and colour vision tests are mandatory, with monthly checks during treatment.
mcqs.question: The antitubercular drug most likely to cause optic neuritis is:

mcqs.explanation: Rifampicin is a red-orange crystalline compound, and its main metabolite desacetylrifampicin is similarly coloured. Both are excreted in urine, tears, saliva, sweat and sputum, staining them orange-red. Patients must be warned before starting — it can permanently stain soft contact lenses.
options: Rifampicin and its major metabolite (desacetylrifampicin) are red-orange coloured compounds excreted in all secretions
It is concentrated in body fluids
It reacts with proteins in fluids
mcqs.question: Rifampicin turns body fluids (urine, tears, sweat) an orange-red colour because:

mcqs.explanation: Isoniazid competes with pyridoxal phosphate (the active form of vitamin B6) for the enzyme pyridoxine phosphokinase and also increases renal pyridoxine excretion. The resulting B6 deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy. Prophylactic pyridoxine 10 mg/day is given with isoniazid, especially to those at high risk (elderly, diabetics, alcoholics, malnourished, HIV positive).
options: Zinc deficiency — prevented by zinc supplementation
Folate deficiency — prevented by folic acid
Pyridoxine (B6) depletion — prevented by co-prescribing pyridoxine 10 mg/day
mcqs.question: Peripheral neuropathy from isoniazid is caused by and prevented by:

mcqs.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, the enzyme that converts acetaldehyde (the first product of ethanol metabolism) to acetate. Acetaldehyde accumulates, causing the unpleasant disulfiram-like reaction: flushing, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension. Alcohol must be avoided during and for 48 hours after treatment.
options: Directly reacts with ethanol in the gut
Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde accumulates → flushing, nausea, palpitations
mcqs.question: Metronidazole causes a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol because it:

mcqs.explanation: Fluoroquinolones trap the covalent DNA-gyrase (or DNA-topo IV) complex in a cleavage state → permanent DNA double-strand breaks → rapid bacterial death (concentration-dependent bactericidal). The human topoisomerases II are ~1000-fold less sensitive.
options: Inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV → DNA strand breaks → bacterial death
mcqs.question: Fluoroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin) are bactericidal because they:

mcqs.explanation: Fungal cell membranes contain ergosterol; human cell membranes contain cholesterol. Amphotericin B binds ergosterol with much higher affinity than cholesterol, explaining its selective fungal toxicity. Its nephrotoxicity arises because renal tubular cells have some ergosterol-like sterols and are exposed to high drug concentrations.
mcqs.question: Amphotericin B is selectively toxic to fungi because it binds ergosterol. The analogous human sterol is:

mcqs.explanation: Acyclovir requires phosphorylation to acyclovir triphosphate (the active inhibitor of viral DNA polymerase). The first phosphorylation step is performed exclusively by herpesvirus-encoded thymidine kinase (TK), which is only present in virus-infected cells. Human kinases cannot perform this step efficiently, giving the drug extraordinary selectivity.
options: It is only absorbed by virus-infected cells
Human kinases do not phosphorylate it even at high concentrations
It binds viral DNA directly without activation
Only virus-infected cells express viral thymidine kinase (TK) which performs the first phosphorylation step, activating the prodrug
mcqs.question: Acyclovir is selectively toxic to virus-infected cells because:

mcqs.explanation: Widespread P. falciparum resistance to chloroquine has developed globally (resistance mutation: pfcrt K76T on chromosome 7). WHO recommends artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) as first-line for falciparum malaria. Chloroquine remains effective for P. vivax and P. ovale in most areas.
options: Widespread P. falciparum resistance has developed, making chloroquine largely ineffective
It is not active against Plasmodium falciparum
It is only active against liver stages
mcqs.question: Chloroquine is NOT used for falciparum malaria in most endemic regions because:

mcqs.explanation: Primaquine and its metabolites generate reactive oxygen species. Normally, reduced glutathione (maintained by G6PD) neutralises these. In G6PD deficiency, oxidative stress is uncompensated → oxidation of Hb to met-Hb, Heinz body formation, and haemolysis of susceptible RBCs.
options: Haemolytic anaemia (oxidative destruction of RBCs) in G6PD-deficient patients
mcqs.question: Primaquine must not be given without first testing for G6PD deficiency because it causes:

mcqs.explanation: Bleomycin causes pulmonary toxicity (pneumonitis → fibrosis) in 10% of patients, which is dose-related and can be fatal. It is unique in that it causes minimal myelosuppression. Monitoring includes regular DLCO (diffusing capacity) and CXR, and total cumulative dose must not exceed safe limits.
mcqs.question: The hallmark unique toxicity of bleomycin (anticancer antibiotic) is:

mcqs.explanation: Hepatic CYP450 activates cyclophosphamide to hydroxycyclophosphamide → phosphoramide mustard (DNA alkylator, the active anticancer metabolite) + acrolein (a toxic byproduct). Acrolein is excreted in the urine and directly damages the bladder urothelium. Mesna (sodium 2-mercaptoethanesulphonate) inactivates acrolein in the urine, preventing cystitis.
options: Acrolein, which is excreted in the urine and is toxic to the bladder epithelium
mcqs.question: Cyclophosphamide causes haemorrhagic cystitis because one of its metabolites is:

mcqs.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, blocking the conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate. This depletes folate cofactors needed for thymidylate and purine synthesis (affecting rapidly dividing normal cells — gut, bone marrow). Folinic acid (5-formyl-THF, leucovorin) bypasses the DHFR block and rescues normal cells while tumour cells (with impaired folate transport) are less able to take it up.
options: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) → depletes tetrahydrofolate → prevents DNA synthesis in normal cells
Causes renal failure that prevents methotrexate excretion
Induces liver enzymes that metabolise folinic acid
mcqs.question: Methotrexate at high doses requires 'folinic acid rescue' because methotrexate:

mcqs.explanation: Vinca alkaloids bind to β-tubulin dimers (at a site different from colchicine) and prevent their polymerisation into the mitotic spindle. Without a functional spindle, chromosomes cannot segregate at metaphase → mitotic arrest and apoptosis. This is cell-cycle specific (M phase).
options: Stabilising the polymerised microtubule (opposite of taxanes)
Binding β-tubulin → preventing microtubule polymerisation → mitotic spindle failure → metaphase arrest
mcqs.question: Vinca alkaloids (vincristine, vinblastine) exert their anticancer effect by:

mcqs.explanation: Doxorubicin causes cumulative, dose-dependent cardiomyopathy (dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure) due to free radical damage to cardiomyocytes. LVEF monitoring is mandatory, and the total lifetime dose must not exceed 450–550 mg/m2. Liposomal doxorubicin reduces cardiotoxicity.
options: Cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy, dose-related) with a maximum lifetime dose of approximately 450–550 mg/m2
mcqs.question: The major adverse effect of doxorubicin that limits cumulative dose is:

mcqs.explanation: Azathioprine is converted to 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP), which is then inactivated by xanthine oxidase (among other enzymes). Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase → 6-MP accumulates → bone marrow suppression and hepatotoxicity. The dose of azathioprine/6-MP must be reduced by 50–75% if allopurinol is added.
options: Xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that metabolises these purine analogues to inactive metabolites → drug accumulation
mcqs.question: Allopurinol significantly raises the toxicity of azathioprine and mercaptopurine because it inhibits:

mcqs.explanation: MDR-TB arises almost entirely from inadequate or incomplete treatment — partial suppression of sensitive strains while resistant mutants survive. DOTS ensures that a healthcare worker or trained observer watches the patient swallow every dose in the intensive phase, eliminating non-adherence as a cause of resistance.
options: Ensuring the correct antibiotic combination is used
Monitoring for adverse drug reactions daily
Preventing the emergence of drug resistance by confirming that every dose is actually swallowed
mcqs.question: DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment Short-course) for tuberculosis is primarily aimed at:

questions.answer:
1. Adrenergic agonists (sympathomimetics) mimic the effects of noradrenaline and adrenaline at adrenergic receptors.
2. Classification by mechanism: (a) Direct acting — act on adrenergic receptors directly: adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, isoprenaline, salbutamol, phenylephrine. (b) Indirect acting — enter the nerve terminal and release stored noradrenaline: amphetamine, ephedrine. (c) Mixed acting — both direct and indirect: ephedrine.
3. Classification by receptor selectivity: (a) Alpha agonists: phenylephrine (α1), clonidine (α2). (b) Beta agonists: isoprenaline (β1+β2), dobutamine (β1), salbutamol (β2). (c) Non-selective (α+β): adrenaline, noradrenaline.
4. Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the principal hormone of the adrenal medulla; it is an agonist at α1, α2, β1, and β2 receptors.
5. Cardiovascular effects: β1 stimulation increases heart rate (chronotropy), force (inotropy) and AV conduction velocity; α1 stimulation constricts skin, splanchnic and renal vessels raising diastolic pressure; β2 stimulation dilates skeletal muscle vessels.
6. Respiratory effects: β2 stimulation relaxes bronchial smooth muscle → bronchodilation; also inhibits mast cell mediator release.
7. Metabolic effects: β2 raises blood glucose (stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis); β3 promotes lipolysis; hypokalaemia at high doses (K+ entry into cells via β2).
8. Central effects: anxiety, tremor, excitement (poor BBB penetration, but indirect effects via periphery).
9. Uses: anaphylaxis and angioedema (drug of choice, 0.5 mg IM); cardiac arrest (IV); acute severe asthma; adjunct to local anaesthetics (reduces bleeding, prolongs action via α1 vasoconstriction); open-angle glaucoma (reduces aqueous production).
10. Adverse effects: palpitations, tachycardia, anxiety, tremor, headache, hypertension, arrhythmias (especially in patients on halothane or non-selective beta blockers).
11. Contraindications: hypertension, severe coronary artery disease, thyrotoxicosis, narrow-angle glaucoma; caution with non-selective beta blockers (unopposed α1 → hypertensive crisis).
12. Routes: IM (thigh) for anaphylaxis; IV for cardiac arrest and severe asthma; SC not recommended (variable absorption); inhalation for asthma.
questions.question: Classify adrenergic agonists with examples. Discuss the mechanism of action, pharmacological effects, uses and adverse effects of adrenaline.

questions.answer:
1. Adrenergic antagonists block adrenergic receptors and reduce sympathetic tone.
2. Classification: (a) Alpha blockers — selective α1: prazosin, doxazosin; non-selective α1+α2: phentolamine, phenoxybenzamine. (b) Beta blockers — non-selective β1+β2: propranolol, pindolol, timolol; selective β1 (cardioselective): atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol; with additional α1 block: carvedilol, labetalol. (c) Alpha-beta combined: carvedilol, labetalol.
3. Beta blockers competitively block β adrenergic receptors, preventing catecholamine binding.
4. Pharmacological effects: reduce heart rate (chronotropy), reduce force (inotropy), slow AV conduction, reduce renin release from juxtaglomerular cells, reduce aqueous humour production.
5. Cardioselective beta blockers (atenolol, bisoprolol) preferentially block β1 at clinical doses, so β2 effects (bronchial, vascular) are largely spared — relatively safer in mild asthma.
6. Drugs with ISA (intrinsic sympathomimetic activity) such as pindolol partially activate the receptor and cause less bradycardia at rest.
7. Propranolol: lipophilic, crosses BBB; uses include migraine prophylaxis, essential tremor, anxiety (stage fright), portal hypertension (reduces hepatic blood flow).
8. Uses of beta blockers: hypertension, stable and unstable angina, arrhythmias (AF rate control, SVT, post-MI arrhythmia), heart failure (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol — reduce mortality), post-MI (reduce infarct size and prevent reinfarction), thyrotoxicosis (control symptoms), phaeochromocytoma (after alpha blockade), glaucoma (timolol eye drops).
9. Adverse effects: bradycardia, AV block, heart failure worsening in acute decompensation, bronchospasm (β2 blockade — most dangerous), cold extremities (β2 blockade in peripheral vasculature), fatigue, impotence, masking of hypoglycaemia signs in diabetics (tachycardia masked; sweating preserved), nightmares and depression with lipophilic drugs.
10. Contraindications: asthma or COPD with bronchoconstriction, uncompensated heart failure, bradycardia, second or third degree heart block, Raynaud's phenomenon, hypoglycaemia-prone type 1 diabetics.
11. Do not stop abruptly — taper over 1–2 weeks to prevent rebound angina and MI.
12. Nursing care: measure apical pulse before each dose and hold if <60 bpm; educate patient not to stop abruptly; monitor blood glucose in diabetics; watch for dyspnoea (bronchospasm); advise about cold extremities and fatigue.
questions.question: Classify adrenergic antagonists. Discuss beta adrenergic blockers — their classification, mechanism, uses, adverse effects, contraindications and nursing care.

questions.answer:
1. Autacoids (from Greek autos = self, akos = remedy) are locally acting substances produced in tissues that act near their site of release; they include histamine, serotonin, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, bradykinin, and platelet activating factor.
2. Histamine is 2-(imidazol-4-yl)ethylamine, formed from L-histidine by L-histidine decarboxylase (cofactor pyridoxal phosphate) and degraded by diamine oxidase and histamine-N-methyltransferase.
3. Sources: mast cells of skin, lung, gut; basophils; enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells of the stomach; histaminergic neurons of the hypothalamus. Release is triggered by IgE-mediated reactions, drugs (morphine, tubocurarine), and direct injury.
4. H1 receptors (Gq, IP3/DAG): bronchial smooth muscle, capillary endothelium, sensory nerves, brain — effects include bronchoconstriction, vasodilation with increased permeability, oedema and itch, wakefulness.
5. H2 receptors (Gs, cAMP): parietal cells, heart, uterus — acid secretion, tachycardia.
6. H3 receptors (Gi): presynaptic autoreceptors in CNS — reduce histamine release.
7. H4 receptors (Gi): eosinophils, mast cells — chemotaxis in inflammation.
8. Classification of H1 antihistamines: (a) First generation — sedating; cross BBB and block muscarinic receptors. Ethanolamines: diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate. Ethylenediamines: tripelennamine. Alkylamines: chlorpheniramine, triprolidine. Piperazines: cyclizine, meclizine. Phenothiazines: promethazine. (b) Second generation — non-sedating; polar, do not cross BBB. Cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine, desloratadine.
9. Mechanism: competitive antagonism at H1 receptors; first generation additionally block muscarinic (dry mouth, urinary retention) and H1 in CNS (sedation).
10. Uses: allergic rhinitis, urticaria and pruritus, drug and insect bite reactions, adjunct in anaphylaxis (after adrenaline), motion sickness (promethazine, cyclizine), vertigo (meclizine), premedication, cough mixtures, insomnia (diphenhydramine).
11. Adverse effects of first generation: sedation (H1 CNS block), dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision, constipation (muscarinic block), dizziness, impaired cognition.
12. Second generation advantages: once daily, non-sedating, fewer anticholinergic effects; preferred for allergic rhinitis in those who must drive or work.
questions.question: Classify autacoids. Describe the pharmacology of histamine with its receptors. Discuss the classification and uses of H1 antihistamines.

questions.answer:
Mechanism: atropine is a competitive antagonist at all muscarinic receptors (M1, M2, M3), blocking the effects of acetylcholine and parasympathetic stimulation.
Pharmacological effects (dose-dependent): 0.5 mg → slight bradycardia (paradoxical, from presynaptic M2 block); 1 mg → dry mouth, tachycardia; 2 mg → tachycardia, mydriasis, dry skin; 5 mg → all the above plus urinary retention, delirium, hyperthermia.
Mnemonic: 'Mad as a hatter (confusion), blind as a bat (mydriasis, cycloplegia), dry as a bone (dry mouth and skin), red as a beet (flushing), hot as a hare (hyperthermia).
Uses: preanesthetic medication (reduces secretions); sinus bradycardia and heart block; organophosphate poisoning (antidote — given until secretions dry up and tachycardia ensues); before neostigmine (blocks muscarinic side effects of neostigmine); ophthalmic mydriasis and cycloplegia; antispasmodic in GI and biliary colic; irritable bowel syndrome.
Adverse effects: tachycardia, urinary retention (prostatic hypertrophy), constipation, dry mouth, blurred vision, photophobia, confusion, hyperthermia.
Contraindications: closed-angle glaucoma (mydriasis blocks drainage angle), benign prostatic hypertrophy (urinary retention), myasthenia gravis (blocks therapeutic acetylcholine), tachyarrhythmias, paralytic ileus.
questions.question: Discuss the pharmacology of atropine — mechanism, pharmacological effects, uses, adverse effects and contraindications.

questions.answer:
Prostaglandins are lipid mediators derived from arachidonic acid. Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; cyclooxygenase (COX) then converts it to cyclic endoperoxides (PGG2, PGH2), which are further processed by specific synthases to prostanoids.
COX-1 is constitutive — present in most tissues; produces prostaglandins that protect the gastric mucosa (PGE2 and PGI2 stimulate mucus and bicarbonate secretion), aggregate platelets (thromboxane A2), and maintain renal blood flow.
COX-2 is inducible — expressed at sites of inflammation and in response to cytokines; produces prostaglandins that mediate pain (PGE2, PGI2 lower pain threshold), fever (PGE2 acts in the hypothalamus), and vasodilation with oedema.
NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac, indomethacin) non-selectively inhibit both COX-1 and COX-2 → anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic effects; but also reduce gastric protection → peptic ulcers and GI bleeding.
Aspirin irreversibly acetylates the active site serine of COX → permanent inhibition for the platelet's lifetime (7–10 days) → antiplatelet effect at low doses (75 mg/day).
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib) spare COX-1 → less GI toxicity, but increased cardiovascular risk (TXA2 still produced, PGI2 reduced → prothrombotic state).
Nursing care: take with food; watch for black or tarry stools; check renal function in elderly; avoid in last trimester of pregnancy; use with PPI in high-risk patients.
questions.question: Discuss prostaglandins and the mechanism of action of NSAIDs on the prostaglandin pathway.

questions.answer:
Classification: (a) Non-selective α1+α2 blockers: phentolamine (competitive, short-acting), phenoxybenzamine (irreversible covalent, long-acting). (b) Selective α1 blockers: prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin.
Mechanism of prazosin: selectively blocks post-synaptic α1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation of both arterioles and veins → fall in peripheral resistance → reduced blood pressure. Because presynaptic α2 receptors (which provide negative feedback on noradrenaline release) are spared, the baroreceptor reflex and noradrenaline feedback remain intact, so reflex tachycardia is less than with non-selective blockers.
Uses of prazosin: hypertension (not first-line alone but useful in combination); benign prostatic hyperplasia (relaxes smooth muscle in prostate capsule and bladder neck → improved urinary flow).
Uses of phentolamine: diagnosis and pre-operative management of phaeochromocytoma; extravasation of vasopressors (local injection reverses ischaemia); hypertensive crisis from MAOI-tyramine interaction.
Adverse effects: first-dose postural hypotension (most important — can cause syncope; advise patient to take first dose lying down or at bedtime); dizziness, palpitations, nasal congestion, oedema.
Nursing education: warn about first-dose hypotension; take first dose at bedtime; rise slowly from bed; avoid standing suddenly.
